title: Ward’s Two Indentures
passage:
John Ward was bound twice. In 1751 he went to a saddler for seven years, with eleven pounds paid down; in 1755 to a whitesmith, for seven years again, and fourteen pounds. Both entries stood in the town clerk’s register of enrolled indentures at Hurstleford, naming Ward’s father, his trade and his parish. Between 1746 and 1771 the clerk enrolled two hundred and eleven bindings, none for any term but seven years, and fifty-seven carried no note that the term was served out. Five names in the book occurred twice, Ward’s among them. The second entries were not continuations: each named a different trade, each ran its seven years from the day of sealing, and each fell three to six years after the first. In three of the five the second premium was the larger sum. Each of the first masters went on enrolling boys of his own for years afterwards. Of the five fathers, two lived in the town, one farmed nine miles off, one combed wool in the next county, and one the clerk left unplaced. He set his fee of two shillings against each enrolment, and twice against Ward’s name.
– Philippa Kembersall

questions.prompt: What is suggested about the five boys who were bound twice?

options.text: They were bound for years beyond the day their first term would have ended.
The five lost their first places when the masters who held them gave up their trades.
They were placed a second time by families living in the town.
The five went into their second trades at a smaller premium than the first had cost.

questions.rationale: TYPE-002, one_inch_inference. The passage states four things and joins none of them: (i) the book holds no term but seven years; (ii) five names occur twice; (iii) the second entries were not continuations — each ran its seven years from the day it was sealed; (iv) each second binding fell three to six years after the one it followed. Three to six is less than seven, so a second term sealed three to six years into a seven-year term must still be running when the first term would have expired, and must run three to six years past it. That is key A. Note what A deliberately does NOT claim: not that the five finished, not that they were made free, not what became of them. The passage says fifty-seven bindings carry no note of service, and the five may be among them; an option that asserted completion would be unsupported. A asserts only the length of the obligation the second indenture created, which the arithmetic of the sealing dates settles on its own. B = the master-failure misread, and the most natural story a reader brings to a broken indenture: the master died or gave up, so the boy had to be placed again. It is defeated in one clause — each of the first masters went on enrolling apprentices of his own for years afterwards, so the trade he practised did not end. C = the local-connections misread, an origins claim that inverts what the record shows: of the five fathers only two lived in the town, one held land nine miles off, one worked in the next county, and one the clerk left unplaced at all. It also smuggles in an agent the passage never names, since nothing says who arranged a second binding. D = the discount-for-damaged-goods misread, and the most economically plausible of the three: a master taking a boy who had already broken one indenture might be expected to ask less. The passage refuses it twice — Ward’s own premium rose from eleven pounds to fourteen, and in three of the five the second premium was the larger sum. Each distractor carries a named flaw a careful reader can point to, and none of them contradicts A, so no pair on the sheet advertises itself as holding the key.

generator_meta.period_detail_note: Checks a period auditor would run. SEVEN-YEAR TERM: the Statute of Artificers 1563 required a minimum seven years and it remained the norm until the repeal of the apprenticeship clauses in 1814, so a book covering 1746-1771 with no term but seven years is right, and the passage makes that invariant explicit because the key depends on it. WHO WAS BOUND TO WHOM: the indenture named the apprentice, the master and the trade, and the boy's father or friends were parties who covenanted and paid; a borough register recording the father's name, trade and parish is standard, and it is the father's abode that makes two entries joinable, which is why the passage says so. WHY A BOROUGH ENROLLED AT ALL: the freedom of a corporate borough came by servitude, so the corporation kept its own enrolment of indentures and charged a fee for it; two shillings is an ordinary clerk's fee. PREMIUMS: eleven and fourteen pounds are inside the ordinary provincial range for craft trades in the 1750s (a few pounds for the humblest trades, tens of pounds for the better ones, hundreds only for merchants and the professions); the passage deliberately uses figures that are unremarkable rather than striking. TRADES: saddler, whitesmith (a finisher and worker of tinned or bright iron, distinct from a blacksmith) and wool-comber are all real eighteenth-century occupations. NON-COMPLETION: fifty-seven of two hundred and eleven, about twenty-seven per cent, is a plausible shortfall for a provincial register - completion rates well under three-quarters are unremarkable in the literature. WHAT THE RECORD WOULD NOT HOLD: it would not record why a boy left, where he went if he left the town, or what a second master thought of him, and the unit asserts none of those. TURNING OVER: assignment of the unexpired term to a new master was the normal remedy when a master died or failed, and the passage marks its ABSENCE explicitly ('The second entries were not continuations'), which is what licenses the key; had they been assignments the arithmetic would not run. AGE: a boy bound at about fourteen in 1751 and bound afresh in 1755 would come out at about twenty-five rather than twenty-one, which is the concrete human content of key A and is well attested for re-bound apprentices.
